question: The Georgian Central Electoral Commission reported that the ruling Georgian Dream party received the highest number of votes (53.92%) in the elections to the Georgian Parliament held on 26 October. This result enabled Georgian Dream to form the government on its own.

However, numerous reports confirming violations of electoral procedures and the unprecedented scale of administrative resources committed by the ruling party undermine the principle of freedom and equality of the electoral process and, consequently, the result of the elections itself.

On 5 November, a court in Tetritskaro declared that votes cast at 30 polling stations in the Lower Kartli region in the south-east of the country were invalid as the principle of voting secrecy had been violated. The President of Georgia, Salome Zourabichvili, has said that she does not recognise the results of the parliamentary elections and has called for protests. In this connection: 1.
Will the Vice-President / High Representative ask Georgia for detailed explanations concerning any allegations of irregularities in the electoral process?
Does the Vice-President / High Representative intend to carry out an independent investigation into the conduct of the parliamentary elections in Georgia?

In the event of further evidence of electoral fraud and the forming of a new parliament on the basis of falsified results, what will be the Commission’s policy towards Georgia, in particular in the context of the country’s efforts thus far to further integrate into the structures of the European Union and NATO?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (21.3.2025) The EU relies on the findings of the International Election Observation Mission led by the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR) with participation of the European Parliament.

Its report highlights serious concerns about the impact of recently adopted electoral legislation, the independence of institutions involved in the election process, and pressure and intimidation on voters, including public employees. These factors compromised the ability of voters to cast their vote freely, without fear of retribution.

The report also raises concerns regarding post-election developments, including insufficient consideration of complaints and the forcible suppression of protests which go against international obligations and standards, including commitments to uphold freedom of assembly. The EU has urged the Georgian authorities to address the reported concerns swiftly, transparently and independently.

This responsibility lies with the Georgian authorities. The EU will continue calling on the Georgian authorities to address the recommendations of the OSCE/ODIHR report promptly, in particular in view of the municipal elections of October 2025. This is crucial to rebuild public trust in the electoral process.

Since June 2024, the EU has responded to Georgia's democratic backsliding with concrete measures and continues to closely monitor the situation. The EU stands with the Georgian people and their choice for a European future.
